0.note: The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

1.q: יָק֣וּם אֱ֭לֹהִים יָפ֣וּצוּ אוֹיְבָ֑י⁠ו וְ⁠יָנ֥וּסוּ מְ֝שַׂנְאָ֗י⁠ו
1.note: By using **Let**, the psalmist is expressing his wish or prayer. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [I desire that God should arise and make his enemies scatter and the ones hating him flee]

These two phrases **let his enemies scatter** and **let the ones hating him flee from his face** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [may all who oppose him scatter and flee]

Here, **from his face** represents being away from God’s presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from before him]

2.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **smoke is driven away** easily and completely by wind, so should God’s enemies be easily and completely driven away. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Scatter them completely, just as smoke is scattered by the wind]

The expression **smoke is driven away** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the wind drives smoke away]

2.q: כְּ⁠הִמֵּ֣ס דּ֭וֹנַג מִ⁠פְּנֵי־אֵ֑שׁ יֹאבְד֥וּ רְ֝שָׁעִ֗ים מִ⁠פְּנֵ֥י אֱלֹהִֽים
2.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **wax melts from the face of fire**, dissolving and disappearing before heat, so will the wicked perish before God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [just as wax dissolves when heat strikes it, let the wicked perish before God]

Here, **from the face of fire** represents being near the front surface of fire. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from the heat of fire]

By using **let**, the psalmist is expressing what he desires or prays will happen. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [the wicked should be destroyed]

The psalmist is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [wicked people]

Here, **from the face of God** represents being away from God’s presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from before God]

3.q: וְֽ⁠צַדִּיקִ֗ים יִשְׂמְח֣וּ יַֽ֭עַלְצוּ לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י אֱלֹהִ֗ים וְ⁠יָשִׂ֥ישׂוּ בְ⁠שִׂמְחָֽה
3.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent sets of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [But let the righteous celebrate joyfully in God’s presence]

The psalmist is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [But let righteous people rejoice]
Here, **to the face of God** represents being in God’s presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before God]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **rejoicing**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [as they rejoice greatly]

4.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [Sing praise to God, making music to him]

The psalmist is using the term **his name** to represent who God is and to refer to God’s reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [who he is]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [lift up a song to the one riding over the plains]

Here the psalmist is speaking of God as if he were **the one riding over the plains**, evoking the image of a powerful warrior or king who commands the open wilderness. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one who moves powerfully through the desert wastelands]

Here, **exult to his face** represents rejoicing in God’s presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [yes, exult before him]

5.note: The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe a father who is characterized by caring for orphans. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [A father to orphans]

Here the psalmist is speaking of God as if he were **A father of orphans**, meaning God cares for and protects those who have no earthly father. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [One who cares for orphans as a father would]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe a judge who is characterized by defending widows. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a defender of widows]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **his holiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [his holy being]

6.note: The psalmist is using the adjective **lonely** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are lonely]

The psalmist uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between those whom God blesses and those who rebel against him. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [However, the ones rebelling dwell in dryness]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if **dryness** were a place where rebels must live, representing the barrenness and hardship of life without God’s blessing. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [dwell in a barren land]

7.note: The psalmist is using the clause **when you went out to the face of your people, when you marched in the wilderness** to describe something that was ongoing. This provides the background for the events he describes in verse 8. Connect this clause to the following verse in a way that makes it clear in your language that this clause is describing something that was ongoing in the background. Alternate translation: [as you went out before your people, as you marched through the wilderness]

See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [when you marched before your people through the wilderness]

Here, **to the face of your people** represents going out in front of and leading the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before your people]

8.note: The psalmist is speaking of **the earth quaked** as if the earth were a living thing that could react with fear. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the earth trembled]

The psalmist is speaking of **the heavens dripped** as if the heavens were a living thing that could pour out rain. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [rain fell from the sky]

Here, **from the face of God** represents being in front of God, that is, in his presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from the presence of God]

8.q: זֶ֥ה סִינַ֑י מִ⁠פְּנֵ֥י אֱ֝לֹהִ֗ים אֱלֹהֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
8.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. The verb “quaked” from the previous clause is implied here. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [this Sinai also quaked, from the face of God, the God of Israel]

Here, **from the face of God** represents being in front of God, that is, in his presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from the presence of God]

The psalmist is not using this possessive form **the God of Israel** to indicate that the Israelites possess or control God. Rather the psalmist is using these words to indicate that God is the one whom Israel worships. Alternate translation: [who is the God whom Israel worships]

9.note: The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe a **rain** that is characterized by **generosities**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [You poured out abundant rainfall]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **generosities**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [A generous rainful]

David is speaking as if the land of Israel were actually Yahweh’s **inheritance**, that is, as if it were something that belonged to him permanently because he inherited it from an ancestor. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the land that belongs to you]

The expression **when it was wearied** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [when it grew weary]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you established** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that God himself is the one who acted. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [indeed, you established it]

10.note: Here the psalmist is speaking as if God’s people were **your flock**, an animal herd cared for by a shepherd. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Your nation]
The pronoun **it** refers to the land, that is, the inheritance mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [in the land]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **goodness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because you are good]

The psalmist is using the adjective **poor** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [for those who are needy]

11.note: The psalmist is using the term **word** to represent the message or command that the Lord spoke. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The Lord speaks his command]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if the women proclaiming good news were **a great army**, a large and powerful fighting force. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the women proclaiming good news are a vast company]

The Hebrew word translated as **the women proclaiming good news** is feminine in form, indicating that those who announced the victory were specifically women. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this explicit. Alternate translation: [the female heralds]

12.note: The psalmist is using the possessive form to mean kings who command armies. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Kings who command armies]

The words **flee** and **they flee** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two words together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [they flee in great haste]

The pronoun **they** refers to the kings, while the pronoun **she** refers to the woman who stays at home. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the kings flee, and the woman who stays at home divides]

13.note: The pronoun you does not refer to God, as in verses 7–10. It is plural, and it refers to Israelite men who stayed back to care for flocks instead of going into battle. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Even if you were among the Israelite men who lay down between the sheepfolds] or [Even if you were among the Israelite men who cared for flocks instead of going into battle]

The psalmist is using **the wings of a dove covered with silver** to represent a dove statue on which the wings are covered with silver. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a dove statue whose wings are covered with silver]

David assumes that his listeners will understand that he is describing the type of plunder that even men who stayed out of battle to care for flocks will receive. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [you will still receive plunder such as a dove statue whose wings are covered with silver]

The expression **covered with silver** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [with a silver covering]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. The word “covered” from the previous clause is implied here. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and its feathers covered with greenness of gold]

14.q: בְּ⁠פָ֘רֵ֤שׂ שַׁדַּ֓י מְלָ֘כִ֤ים בָּ֗⁠הּ תַּשְׁלֵ֥ג בְּ⁠צַלְמֽוֹן
14.note: The word **When** indicates that the scattering of kings and the snowfall on Zalmon happened at the same time. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could describe the time relationship more explicitly. Alternate translation: [As Shaddai scattered kings in it, it snowed on Zalmon]

The pronoun **it** refers to the land, the region where the battle took place. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [in the place where the enemy army had assembled]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if the whitened, fleeing armies were **it snowed on Zalmon**, comparing their scattered flight to snowfall blanketing a dark mountain. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the battlefield was white, like snow on Zalmon]

15.note: The psalmist is using **a mountain of God** as a common expression of the culture to mean “a very great mountain.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a magnificent mountain]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe a mountain that is characterized by having many peaks. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a many-peaked mountain]

16.q: לָ֤⁠מָּה ׀ תְּֽרַצְּדוּ⁠ן֮ הָרִ֪ים גַּבְנֻ֫נִּ֥ים הָ⁠הָ֗ר חָמַ֣ד אֱלֹהִ֣ים לְ⁠שִׁבְתּ֑⁠וֹ
16.note: The psalmist is using the question form to assert that God has chosen Mount Zion as his dwelling place, not the impressive Mount Bashan. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You other mountains and peaks should not look enviously at the mountain God desired for his dwelling!]

The psalmist is speaking of **mountains, peaks** as if they were living things that could feel envy. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Why do you look enviously, O rugged mountains]

The psalmist is speaking to **mountains, peaks** that he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about God’s choice of Zion. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about the mountains. Alternate translation: [many-peaked mountains] or [dwellers among the many-peaked mountains]
The pronoun **his** refers to God. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [for God’s dwelling]

17.note: Here the psalmist is speaking as if God’s overwhelming power were **the chariotry of God**, a vast military force of chariots. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The armies of God]

The psalmist says **two myriads, thousands of repetition** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [tens of thousands upon thousands]
The pronoun **them** refers to the chariots/myriads. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [is among the chariots]

18.note: Here the psalmist is speaking of God’s victory as if it were **ascended to the height**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You have risen to supremacy]

The psalmist is using **you have taken captivity captive** as a common expression of the culture to mean that he has taken a great multitude of prisoners. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you have led a host of captives]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **captivity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [captives]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [among people]

Here, **that Yah God might dwell there** marks the entire preceding action of ascending, taking captives, and receiving gifts as the goal or purpose of those acts—namely, that God would establish his dwelling. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [so that Yah God might dwell there]

19.note: The expression **Blessed be** is a passive verbal form. The psalmist is expressing his desire to praise the Lord. If it would be unnatural to use that form for this purpose, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [We bless the Lord] or [Let me praise the Lord]

The psalmist is repeating the word **Day** in order to intensify the meaning or the emotion that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Day after day]

Here the psalmist is speaking of the Lord’s support as if he **bears** a load on behalf of his people. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he carries our burdens]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **the God** who is characterized by saving. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the God who delivers us]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the God who rescues us]

20.q: הָ֤⁠אֵ֣ל ׀ לָ⁠נוּ֮ אֵ֤ל לְֽ⁠מוֹשָׁ֫ע֥וֹת וְ⁠לֵ⁠יהוִ֥ה אֲדֹנָ֑⁠י לַ֝⁠מָּ֗וֶת תּוֹצָאֽוֹת
20.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [God is to us a God of salvations; indeed, Yahweh the Lord delivers us from death]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvations**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a God who saves]

Here the psalmist is speaking of escaping death as if it were **exits from** a place called death. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [ways of escaping from death]

21.note: The psalmist is using one part of a person, **the head**, to mean all parts of his enemies in the act of being defeated. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [will crush his enemies]

The psalmist is leaving out the verb **crush** that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply this word from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [crushing the pate of hair of the one walking ahead in his trespasses]

Here the psalmist is speaking of persisting in sin as if it were **walking ahead** in a direction of one’s own choosing. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one who continues in his trespasses]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **trespasses**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [who continues trespassing against God]

The pronoun **his** in “his enemies” refers to God, while the pronoun **his** in “his trespasses” refers to the enemy. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [God’s enemies … in the enemy’s trespasses]

22.note: The psalmist is using this possessive form to mean the deepest part of the sea. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [from the deep sea]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. The object “them” (referring to the enemies) is implied. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [I will bring them back from Bashan, I will bring them back from the depths of the sea]

The psalmist is referring to all places by naming two extremes, **from Bashan** (high ground) and **from the depths of the sea** (the lowest depths). If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from the heights … from the depths]

23.note: Here, **so that your foot may smash in blood** marks the purpose of the Lord’s bringing the enemies back. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [in order that your foot may smash in blood]

Here the psalmist is speaking of total victory over enemies as if it were to **smash in blood** with one’s foot. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your foot may trample over the defeated enemies]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. A verb such as “will lick” is implied. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [“the tongue of your dogs will taste its portion from the enemies”]

The psalmist is using one part of the dogs, their **tongue**, to mean the dogs in the act of licking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your dogs will lick]
The pronoun **your** in both “your foot” and “your dogs” refers to God’s people, Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Israel’s foot … Israel’s dogs]

24.q: רָא֣וּ הֲלִיכוֹתֶ֣י⁠ךָ אֱלֹהִ֑ים הֲלִ֘יכ֤וֹת אֵלִ֖⁠י מַלְכִּ֣⁠י
24.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [They see your processions, God—the triumphal march of my God and king]

The pronoun **They** has an unclear referent here; it may refer to the worshipers in Israel generally. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The people see your processions]

25.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. The verb “go” from the first clause is implied. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [the ones playing stringed instruments go behind]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. The verb “go” from the first clause is implied. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [maidens playing timbrels go in the midst]

26.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. The verb “Bless” from the first line is implied. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [bless Yahweh, you from the fountain of Israel]

Here the psalmist is speaking of the origin of the people of Israel as if it were a **fountain**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you who come from the stock of Israel]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe a fountain that is characterized by being Israel’s source or origin. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Israel’s source]

27.note: The psalmist is using the adjective **littlest** as a noun to mean the smallest tribe. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the least significant]
The pronoun **them** refers to the tribes of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [ruling the tribes]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [there are the princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali]

27.q: בִּנְיָמִ֨ן & שָׂרֵ֣י יְ֭הוּדָה & שָׂרֵ֥י זְ֝בֻל֗וּן שָׂרֵ֥י נַפְתָּלִֽי
27.note: Here, **Benjamin**, **the princes of Judah**, **the princes of Zebulun**, and **the princes of Naphtali** represent the leaders of those tribes. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the leaders of Benjamin … the chiefs of Judah … the chiefs of Zebulun … the chiefs of Naphtali]

28.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how strong you are]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please show your strength, God]
The pronoun **You** refers to God. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [God, you have done this for us]
In both uses, the pronoun **Your** refers to Israel being addressed. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Israel’s God has commanded Israel’s strength]

29.q: מֵֽ֭⁠הֵיכָלֶ⁠ךָ עַל־יְרוּשָׁלִָ֑ם לְ⁠ךָ֤ יוֹבִ֖ילוּ מְלָכִ֣ים שָֽׁי
29.note: The word translated as **Because** indicates that what follows is a reason for the result described. If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the first phrase gives the reason for the result that the second phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Kings will bring a gift to you, for your temple stands over Jerusalem]

Here, **your temple** represents God’s presence and dwelling place. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Because of your dwelling place]

30.note: This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please rebuke the beast of the reed]

Here the psalmist is speaking of Egypt as if Egypt were **the beast of the reed**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the enemy from the reeds]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if powerful rulers were **the mighty** and the peoples under them were **the calves**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the assembly of the powerful leaders with the peoples under them]

The psalmist is using this possessive form to mean the assembly that consists of mighty ones. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the assembly made up of mighty rulers]

The psalmist is using the adjective **mighty** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the mighty rulers]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **calves** that are characterized by belonging to **the peoples**—that is, the subject nations. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the peoples’ young warriors]

30.q: מִתְרַפֵּ֥ס בְּ⁠רַצֵּי־כָ֑סֶף בִּזַּ֥ר עַ֝מִּ֗ים קְרָב֥וֹת יֶחְפָּֽצוּ
30.note: The pronoun **himself** and **He** are ambiguous in this context; they may refer to God scattering the enemy, or to the beast humbling itself before God. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the beast humbling itself with pieces of silver. God scatters the peoples who delight in battles]

31.note: The psalmist is speaking of **Cush** as if it were a person who could stretch out its hands toward God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people of Cush will eagerly bring offerings to God]

The psalmist is using **will make its hands run to God** as a common expression of the culture to mean “will hasten to bring offerings to God.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [will quickly bring tribute to God]
The pronoun **its** refers to Cush the nation. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [its own hands]

Here, **its hands** represents the offerings and tribute that Cush’s people bring. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [its tribute]

32.note: The psalmist is speaking to **Kingdoms of the earth** that he knows cannot literally hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about the worship of God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about the kingdoms of the earth. Alternate translation: [All the kingdoms of the world should sing to God]
See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [sing praises to the Lord God]

33.note: Here the psalmist is speaking of God as if he were **the rider on the heavens, of the heavens of antiquity**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to him who rules over the ancient skies]
The psalmist is using this possessive form to mean the highest and most ancient heavens. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the highest ancient heavens]

The psalmist is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Listen! he utters with his voice, a voice of power]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **power**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a powerful voice]

The psalmist is repeating forms of the word **voice** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [with his great, powerful voice]

34.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how strong he is]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **majesty**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [his majestic nature]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and his mighty rule]

Here, **in the clouds** represents the heavenly realm where God displays his power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the heavens above]

35.note: The psalmist switches to addressing Yahweh directly for this line for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the third person for consistency. Alternate translation: [God is fearsome from his sanctuary]

Here, **your sanctuary** represents the place where God dwells and from which he makes his power known. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from your holy dwelling place]

The psalmist is not using this possessive form **The God of Israel** to indicate that the Israelites possess or control God. Rather the psalmist is using these words to indicate that God is the one whom Israel worships. Alternate translation: [You are the God whom Israel worships]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **strength** and **forces**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the power to be strong and courageous]

The terms **strength** and **forces** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [great power and might]

The expression **Blessed be** is a passive verbal form. The psalmist is expressing his desire to praise Yahweh. If it would be unnatural to use that form for this purpose, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I bless God] or [Let me praise God]
